title: Job Tracker
problem: Job seekers need one place to record applications, follow their pipeline and find the next role to follow up.
architecture: Next.js App Router renders the overview and applications on the server. Client components handle forms and filters. Server Actions use Zod and ownership checks, with NextAuth sessions and Prisma persistence in PostgreSQL.
decisions: Scope database operations to the authenticated user.
Validate writes on the server and normalize malformed filter inputs before rendering.
highlights: Sign in and find an application using company search and status filters.
Edit its status, save and reload to confirm persistence.
Try an empty company field, then submit a valid application.
outcome: The source handoff records schema and seed checks, TypeScript, lint, a production build and browser checks for login, validation, filters and persisted edits.
constraints: The repository is unavailable to anonymous visitors. Public source access and hosted demos are pending.
There is no automated project test suite. Lint records one profile image warning.
Running the demo requires PostgreSQL and the local configuration described in the source README.
shortSummary: Track applications from submission to interview and offer, with authenticated editing and focused filters.
demoSetup:
cd job-tracker
npm ci
# Start the isolated PostgreSQL demo using the source README.
# Copy .env.example to .env and configure local values.
npm run db:push
node --env-file=.env prisma/seed.mjs
npm run dev -- --port 3036

title: Ecommerce Analytics
problem: Retail analysts need metric definitions they can reconcile to SQL while exploring dates and shipping markets.
architecture: PostgreSQL 17 stores the retail model and deterministic seed. A Node server executes a read-only SQL report and caches an aggregate snapshot. Native browser modules filter daily and market totals locally.
decisions: Keep storewide cart conversion independent of the shipping-market filter.
Define net revenue as gross sales minus full refunds and expose daily values for reconciliation.
highlights: Apply July 1–7, 2026 and Portugal, then expand the daily chart values.
Switch to all markets and compare revenue while cart conversion stays fixed.
Open Market breakdown and select a market while retaining the date range.
outcome: The latest source handoff records five metric tests, all 14 SQL queries, integrity and inventory concurrency checks, plus Chrome filtering, drill-down, retry and mobile checks.
constraints: The demo reads a snapshot cached until the server restarts.
The fictional seed uses one EUR reporting currency and full refunds attributed to the original order date.
Cart conversion is storewide because unconverted carts have no shipping market. Public source access and hosting are pending.
shortSummary: Reconcile revenue, refunds and conversion, then explore shipping markets and daily trends backed by SQL.

title: Core Banking Ledger
problem: Transfers must remain balanced and authorized when requests repeat or competing sessions debit the same account.
architecture: PostgreSQL stores immutable double-entry journals, posting legs and audit records. Controlled functions calculate balances from the ledger. The loopback Node transfer desk calls the same posting functions as the terminal walkthrough.
decisions: Calculate authoritative balances from posting legs instead of a separately mutable balance column.
Accept matching retry references only for the same authorized principal and payload.
highlights: Post a fictional EUR 25.99 transfer and inspect both ledger legs.
Retry the transfer and confirm that the balance changes once.
Reject an overdraft, then create a compensating reversal with audit history.
outcome: The source handoff records four SQL contract suites, two concurrent transfer scenarios, eight reporting queries and an upgrade preserving record counts. Chrome covered posting, retries, overdraft rejection, reversal, recovery and mobile layout.
constraints: The browser desk requires local PostgreSQL and listens on loopback.
FX is outside the demo. Existing compensating service reversals can create a negative balance.
The repository is unavailable anonymously. Public source access and hosting remain pending.
shortSummary: Post a transfer once, retry it safely, reject an overdraft and inspect an audited reversal.
demoSetup:
cd core-banking-ledger/core-banking-ledger
# Use an isolated Compose project and free database port as documented.
docker compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 600
node scripts/web-demo.mjs

Separate browser simulations from acquisition and actuator control, with visible units and calibration assumptions.

Dashboard: try partial readings and link dropout, then switch metric and imperial units.

Use common postdominators to identify shared continuations.
Clear stale output after edits and discard delayed responses.

title: MiniLang Interpreter
shortSummary: A TypeScript language pipeline with lexical environments, recursion, closures and a bounded browser playground.

architecture: A lexer feeds a recursive-descent parser and tree-walk interpreter. The browser runs the actual interpreter in a disposable worker; the CLI provides a persistent REPL.
decisions: Give blocks child environments and separate AND/OR precedence.
Validate native arity/types and propagate returns explicitly.
Bound visits, call depth and output; terminate browser workers on timeout.
highlights: Inspect editable examples including factorial and returned counter closures.
Display tokens/statement counts, output and language errors; preserve/reset REPL state.
outcome: 62 interpreter tests, type checks, CLI/REPL checks, production build and browser examples passed.
constraints: Educational language: no arrays/objects, modules or JavaScript interop; numbers use JavaScript floating-point behavior.
Worker limits are demo safeguards, not a hardened hostile-code sandbox or memory quota.
Manual Stop was not independently confirmed; interpreter-budget termination and subsequent recovery were verified.

title: Sfera Tag Scanner
shortSummary: A Kotlin Android inventory app with a synthetic-input browser companion powered by shared reference, quantity and duplicate rules.
problem: Clothing-tag references must preserve leading zeros, distinguish exact duplicates from color variants and reject invalid stock operations.
architecture: The Android source uses Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Hilt and Room, with CameraX and ML Kit image-input paths and basic Apache POI spreadsheet helpers. The separate browser companion calls a loopback Kotlin HTTP server compiling the actual InventoryRules.kt and SferaCode.kt. Its inventory and movement adapter is server-side and in memory; it does not run Room or reproduce the Android interface.
decisions: Share platform-independent Kotlin reference, quantity and duplicate rules with Android rather than reimplementing them in JavaScript.
Correct status filtering, reject malformed references, invalid quantities, duplicate entries and repeated exits.
Make unfinished Bluetooth/USB/NFC RFID adapters explicitly report unsupported instead of claiming a successful connection.
Keep the companion synthetic and loopback-only, with a bounded 128 MB Java heap and no API credentials.
highlights: Inspect a dotted reference while retaining leading zeros; distinguish a color variant from an exact duplicate.
Companion inventory supports synthetic entry, full-reference exit, movement history, search and status filtering.
Restore the Gradle wrapper and remove generated Android build products from Git tracking; update the basic spreadsheet dependency without claiming native compatibility verification.
outcome: Preparation passed 18 actual Kotlin core assertions and real Chromium workflow/mobile checks. Integration verifies the running companion without resetting existing inventory. Native Gradle configuration reached SDK discovery and stopped because the Android SDK is missing.
constraints: Native Android build remains blocked by the missing SDK. Camera capture, physical OCR, optional remote image extraction, Room persistence and device file access were not verified.
RFID is unfinished: no tested reader connection, EPC mapping or hardware compatibility is claimed.
Companion inventory/history are server-side in memory, not browser storage. State resets on server restart or explicit sample reset; there is no authentication or persistence.
Exit marks the entire reference out, not a partial sale. Native save/movement transactions and failure recovery still need integration tests.
Spreadsheet helpers read the first worksheet/seven fields and create a new workbook; they do not preserve macros, quantities/status/history or provide full inventory sync/backup.
No affiliation, commissioning, individual contribution narrative, production deployment or business outcome is inferred.

title: ConfigCraft
shortSummary: Inspect and convert JSON, YAML and dotenv in a browser workbench with validation and structured navigation.
problem: Developers need to inspect configuration structure and convert supported formats without sending file contents to a server.
architecture: React and Vite share a parser and serialization layer between the editor, validation, structure tree and conversion actions. Drafts remain in browser memory.
decisions: Reject duplicate JSON keys, unsafe numeric values, YAML aliases and unsupported tags.
Use JSON Pointer paths and one in-memory draft per format to keep inspection and editing consistent.
highlights: Remove a closing brace and inspect validation feedback, then restore the document.
Convert the staging configuration to YAML, download it and reopen it as JSON.
Inspect dotenv string values and duplicate-assignment warnings.
constraints: Validation covers syntax and representable values, without an application-specific schema.
Files are limited to 256 KiB and 70 nesting levels. Formatting, quoting and YAML comments can change during conversion.
Drafts are discarded on reload.

title: Local-First DB Engine
shortSummary: Save documents offline, inspect an IndexedDB outbox and reconcile changes with a local sync service.
problem: Offline-capable tools need local writes and a visible sync history when the server is unavailable or data conflicts.
architecture: A TypeScript document library commits local changes and outbox operations together in IndexedDB. Express accepts typed sync batches and returns snapshots and conflict results.
decisions: Commit a document and its queued operation in one browser transaction.
Deduplicate acknowledged operation IDs in the running server and expose the selected conflict strategy per batch.
highlights: Load the fictional Field Station collection with sync paused.
Edit Tern Point, save locally and reload to inspect the queued version.
Resume sync and compare the acknowledged document with the server snapshot.
constraints: The demo server stores documents, acknowledgements and conflict history in memory, so restart loses that server state.
Batches can partially commit. There is no restart-persistent operation journal or multi-process file lock.
The browser uses HTTP sync and does not subscribe to push updates.

title: CSV Cleaner
shortSummary: Clean UTF-8 contact rows and report duplicate IDs and invalid records.
problem: Small contact exports need repeatable validation and a separate rejection report.
architecture: A Python standard-library CLI parses contact CSV, normalizes IDs and writes accepted rows to stdout and diagnostics to stderr.
decisions: Retain the first valid row for each normalized positive ID.
Return processing errors separately from row-level rejection results.
highlights: Run the synthetic contacts example.
Inspect the two accepted rows and the duplicate and invalid-email report.
constraints: The input header is fixed to id,name,email. Email checks cover basic form.
Rejected rows can coexist with successful processing; malformed input and unreadable files return status 2.

title: Log Analyzer
shortSummary: Summarize log severity counts and preserve malformed source line numbers.
problem: A small application log needs a predictable summary and a clear list of malformed entries.
architecture: A Python standard-library CLI validates ISO timestamps and supported severity levels, then emits ordered JSON counts and malformed line numbers.
decisions: Always emit all five severity levels, including zero counts.
Keep strict malformed-line failure separate from input or command errors.
highlights: Run the sample log and inspect two INFO, one WARNING and one ERROR entry.
Add --strict to report malformed input through exit status 1 while retaining the report.
constraints: Input uses TIMESTAMP LEVEL message and five supported severity names.
This is a local file summary, without live ingestion, alerting or distributed log storage.
